transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… I suppose what finally pushed me to come in is that I’ve gotten sort of stuck in these little routines, and I know they sound small when I say them out loud, but they’re starting to interfere. Like, if I handle my wrist brace, I’ll wash my hands again afterward, even if I’ve already washed them and nothing is really dirty. And before I leave the house, I’ll check the stove, and then the front door, and then sometimes I go back and check them again.

There’s also this counting I do silently in my head, sort of going through steps before I can leave. It’s not dramatic, exactly, but it slows me down. I’ll know, rationally, that I’ve done enough, but I still feel pulled to repeat it. And lately it’s been making me late, which is embarrassing at my age, honestly. I just… I don’t want these little habits taking over more than they already have.
Do you have any recurring thoughts that disturb you or feel intrusive?

Yes… yes, I do. It’s not like I sit there and decide to think these things. They just sort of barge in, usually when I’m doing something ordinary, like reading at home, or getting ready to go in for a museum shift. I’ll suddenly get this ugly little thought that maybe I left something unsafe, or I touched something unclean, or somehow I’ve put someone at risk.

And the frustrating part is that I know, in the sensible part of my mind, that it’s probably completely out of proportion. I can tell myself, “You didn’t do anything dangerous,” or “That’s not actually dirty,” but the thought doesn’t leave politely just because I’ve reasoned with it. It sort of sits there and nags at me, and then I feel I have to do something to settle it. It’s embarrassing to admit, because it sounds so excessive when I say it out loud, but yes, they do feel intrusive.
Do you experience any physical sensations, like tension or restlessness, when these intrusive thoughts occur?

I’m not sure I’ve noticed anything very specific in my body, to be honest. I mean, I can tell I’m uneasy when the thought is there, but whether that’s tension or restlessness in a clear physical sense… I don’t know. I haven’t really paid attention to it that way.

It’s more that the thought feels bothersome and I want it resolved. I might feel keyed up, I suppose, but I couldn’t say, “Oh, my shoulders tighten,” or “I feel it in my chest,” not with any confidence. I’m sorry, that’s probably not very helpful, but I haven’t really sorted out the physical side of it.
Do you feel like these intrusive thoughts are a part of who you are, or do they feel like they're coming from outside of yourself?

They feel like they’re coming from me, if that makes sense—not from outside, not like a voice or anything like that. It’s my own mind producing them, which is part of what makes it so frustrating, because I’ll be sitting there reading at home, or getting ready to go in for a museum shift, and this ugly little thought just barges in: What if I left something unsafe? What if I touched something unclean? What if I’ve somehow put someone at risk?

And I know perfectly well, or at least the reasonable part of me knows, that it’s out of proportion. It doesn’t feel like “someone else” is putting it there. It feels like my own thought, just one I don’t want and don’t agree with. That’s the odd thing—I can recognize it as mine and still feel almost ambushed by it.
Have you been avoiding any situations, places, or activities because of these intrusive thoughts or rituals?

Yes… to some extent. I wouldn’t say I’ve stopped living my life or anything as dramatic as that. I’m still managing on my own, I get myself where I need to go most of the time, and I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is.

But the routines before leaving the house have definitely interfered. There have been mornings when I’m trying to get out to the museum for a docent shift, and I get caught up checking or making sure things feel settled, and then suddenly I’m late. Not terribly late every time, but late enough that I feel embarrassed and flustered when I arrive.

And I have skipped a few museum events, too—not because I didn’t want to go, exactly, but because getting out the door started to feel like too much effort. It’s as if the whole process becomes loaded, and I think, “Oh, never mind, it’s easier just not to go.” I don’t like admitting that, because the museum is important to me, and I don’t want these habits deciding what I do. But yes, they have made me avoid a few things.
How much distress do these intrusive thoughts typically cause you?

They’re distressing, yes, but I’d say not overwhelmingly so most of the time. It’s more like… an ugly little thought barges in and won’t let me simply go on with what I was doing. I’ll be reading at home, for example, and suddenly I’m thinking, did I leave something unsafe? Or I’ll be getting ready to go to a museum shift and it’s, what if I touched something unclean, or somehow put someone at risk?

And I do know, in the sensible part of my mind, that it’s out of proportion. I can say to myself, “This is not reasonable, you don’t need to be this concerned.” But it still creates this nagging distress, this unsettled feeling, like I can’t quite relax until I’ve dealt with it somehow.

So… mild to moderate, maybe? It bothers me and interrupts me, definitely. But I’m not in a complete panic every time. It’s more persistent and wearing than dramatic.
Do you feel like you have to perform these rituals, like checking the stove or counting, in order to reduce your anxiety or prevent something bad from happening?

Yes, I suppose that’s exactly what it feels like, even though part of me is embarrassed to put it that plainly. It isn’t that I truly believe, in a clear-headed way, that if I don’t check the stove one more time the house will definitely burn down, or if I don’t wash my hands again after adjusting my wrist brace something terrible will happen. I know I’ve already done enough.

But in the moment, there’s this pressure—almost like I can’t quite move on until I’ve completed the little routine. I’ll wash my hands, then touch or handle the brace, and then I feel pulled to wash them again, even if I know there’s no real reason. Or I’ll check the stove and the front door before leaving, and then I’m halfway through getting ready and I think, did I really check it properly? So I go back and look again.

And the counting is similar. Before I leave, I sometimes silently count through steps in my head, like I’m making sure everything has been accounted for. It gives me a bit of relief, I suppose, or at least it quiets that anxious feeling for the moment. But then it also makes me late, which is maddening, because I can see what’s happening and still feel like I have to finish it before I can walk out the door.
When you perform these rituals, such as checking the stove or counting, are you trying to prevent something specific from happening or are you just trying to feel less anxious in general?

It’s a bit of both, I think, though if I’m being honest, it’s often less specific than it probably sounds. With the stove and the front door, there is a kind of specific worry underneath it—like, what if I left something on, what if the door isn’t really secure, what if something happens because I was careless. I don’t necessarily picture some detailed disaster every time, but there’s that sense of needing to make sure.

With the counting before I leave, that’s harder to explain. That’s more like trying to get a feeling that everything has been gone through properly. I’ll silently count through steps in my head, almost like I’m checking off that I’ve done what I’m supposed to do, and if it doesn’t feel complete, I get stuck. It’s not always that I think, “If I don’t count this way, this exact bad thing will happen.” It’s more that I feel unsettled and can’t quite leave.

And with the handwashing after handling my wrist brace, again, I know I’ve already done enough much of the time. But I’ll handle it, or adjust it, and then I feel like I need to wash again just to feel right about it. So yes, sometimes it’s tied to preventing something, and sometimes it’s just trying to quiet that anxious, unfinished feeling. The problem is that all these little routines add up, and then I’m late even though I knew, really, that I’d already checked or washed enough.
Have these habits and intrusive thoughts significantly impacted your ability to work or maintain relationships?

Yes… though I’d say it’s not completely derailed my life or anything like that. I’m still managing on my own. I live independently, I get myself where I need to go most of the time, and I’m not working now, so it’s not as though I’m missing a job every morning.

But it has affected my docent work at the museum. That’s probably where it shows up most clearly. I’ll be trying to get out the door for a shift, and the checking and rechecking can eat up more time than I expect. I’ll think, “All right, just one more look,” and then somehow I’m still not settled, and then I’m late. Not terribly late every single time, but enough that I notice it and feel embarrassed walking in.

And I’ve skipped a few museum events too, which bothers me because I do enjoy them. It’s not that I didn’t want to go. It’s more that the process of getting out the door started to feel like too much—too many steps, too much uncertainty, too much of that feeling that I hadn’t done everything properly. So I’ve talked myself out of going, which is a shame.

As for relationships, I wouldn’t say it’s caused some dramatic falling-out with anyone. But it does make me less available sometimes, I suppose, because if I’m late or I cancel, people may not fully understand why. I tend not to explain all the details because it feels a bit foolish when I hear myself say it out loud.
Have you noticed any significant problems in your relationships with family or friends due to these habits and thoughts?

With family or friends, not in a major dramatic way, no. I’m still managing on my own, and I don’t think anyone would say I’ve become completely unreliable or anything like that.

Where it shows up more is around the museum. I’ve been late to docent shifts because getting out the door turns into this whole drawn-out process, and by the time I’ve finished making sure everything feels settled, I’ve lost more time than I meant to. And I have skipped a few museum events altogether, not because I didn’t want to go, but because the thought of going through all those steps just felt like too much that day.

So I suppose it affects relationships indirectly. If I’m late, or if I don’t show up to something, people may not understand why, and I feel embarrassed about that. But I wouldn’t say it’s caused a serious rift with family or friends. It’s more that it makes me less present or dependable than I’d like to be.
Do you feel like your rituals are specifically aimed at preventing harm to yourself or others?

Not exactly in a clear, direct way every time. With the stove or the front door, yes, there’s some of that—like I’m trying to make sure I haven’t left something unsafe or made some careless mistake. But most of the time it doesn’t feel as organized as, “I must do this or someone will be harmed.”

What brings me in is more that I get stuck in these little routines. I wash my hands again after handling my wrist brace, even when part of me knows I’ve already washed enough. I recheck the stove and the front door. I silently count through the steps before I leave, almost to make sure everything has been done properly. And if it doesn’t feel right or complete, I have trouble moving on.

So I suppose there is a fear of something being wrong underneath it, but a lot of it is just this nagging need to do it again until I feel settled. And that’s what’s started causing problems—because even when I know I’ve done enough, I keep repeating things, and then I end up late.
Do you feel like your rituals are specifically aimed at preventing harm to yourself or others?

I think I may have said part of this already, but… no, not always in the sense of, “If I don’t do this, someone will definitely be hurt.” It’s more that I get caught in the routines themselves.

What brings me in, really, is that I’ve gotten stuck doing these little repeated things. I’ll wash my hands again after handling my wrist brace, even if I know perfectly well I washed them already. Or I’ll go back and check the stove, then the front door, and then sometimes I’m not quite satisfied and I’ll check again. Before I leave, I’ll silently count through the steps in my head, almost like I’m trying to make sure the whole sequence has been completed properly.

And the frustrating part is that I do often know I’ve done enough. I can even tell myself, “You’ve checked it, it’s fine, you can go now.” But it doesn’t feel finished, somehow. So I repeat it, and then suddenly I’ve lost time and I’m running late. So it’s not only about preventing harm, exactly—it’s more that I can’t seem to let the routine stop when it should.
Do you have any obsessive thoughts or compulsions that are focused on symmetry or exactness?

Exactness, maybe, but not really symmetry in the sense of needing objects lined up or balanced-looking. I don’t find myself arranging things on a table until they’re perfectly even, or anything like that.

For me it’s more that a sequence has to feel complete. Before I leave, I’ll silently count through what I’ve done—stove, door, whatever else—and if I lose my place or it doesn’t feel quite finished, I’ll start over or check again. It’s not that the number itself is so important, exactly, but the routine has to feel settled before I can move on.

And that’s where I get stuck. I’ll wash my hands again after handling my wrist brace, even when I know I already did it. I’ll recheck the stove and front door even though I can remember checking them. It’s almost like my mind won’t accept that it’s done unless I go through it the “right” way, and then I end up late because I’ve spent all that time trying to get that finished feeling.
Do you believe that something bad will happen to you or someone else if you don't complete these rituals?

Yes… or, well, I suppose that’s the uncomfortable part. I don’t exactly believe it in a rational way. If you asked me plainly, sitting here, “Do you truly think something terrible will happen if you don’t do it?” I’d probably say no, not really. I know it’s out of proportion.

But when I’m in the middle of it, it feels different. I’ll be at home reading, or getting ready to go in for a museum shift, and this ugly little thought barges in—like, what if I left something unsafe, or what if I touched something unclean and then spread it somewhere, or what if I somehow put someone else at risk without realizing it. It’s not always a full, logical thought. It’s more like a jolt of doubt that won’t leave me alone.

So I don’t think I believe it completely, but I feel pressured by it. I get this sense that if I don’t go back and make sure, or don’t redo the thing, then I’m being careless. And even though another part of me knows perfectly well that the worry is exaggerated, it’s hard to just walk away from it.
Do you think the bad things you worry about are more likely to happen to you or to someone else?

I think… more often it’s about someone else, or at least the possibility that I’ve put someone else at risk without realizing it. Not usually a specific person, exactly. It’s more this broad, unpleasant thought that I may have left something unsafe, or touched something unclean, and then somehow carried that risk outward.

Like I’ll be sitting at home reading, perfectly ordinary moment, and suddenly the thought barges in: what if I didn’t leave things properly, what if something is unsafe? Or if I’m getting ready for a museum shift, I’ll think, what if I touched something unclean and then bring that with me, or pass it along somehow. I know, when I say it out loud, it sounds out of proportion. I do know that.

But in the moment it doesn’t feel like a calm calculation of risk. It feels like this little alarm going off, as if I’d be careless if I didn’t take it seriously. So I suppose the worry is less, “Something bad will happen to me,” and more, “What if because of me something bad happens to someone else?”
Do you often worry that your actions or omissions might directly cause harm to someone else?

Yes, that’s probably the central worry, if I’m being honest. It’s not usually that I think I’m in danger myself. It’s more this awful thought that I might have done something—or failed to do something—and because of that someone else could be affected.

I’ll be doing something ordinary, like reading at home, and suddenly the thought just barges in: what if I left something unsafe? Or I’ll be getting ready to go to a museum shift and think, what if I touched something unclean and I’m bringing it with me somehow? It’s not even always a clear, sensible chain of events. It’s just this ugly little jolt of doubt, like I’ve overlooked something important and now someone else might be at risk.

And I do know, perfectly well, that it’s out of proportion. I can say that sitting here. But in the moment, it feels hard to dismiss, because it comes with this feeling that if I ignore it, I’m being careless. So yes, I do worry that my actions or omissions could directly cause harm, even when part of me knows the worry doesn’t really make sense.
Do you often worry about coming into contact with germs or contaminated substances?

Yes, I do, though it isn’t always as straightforward as, “Oh, I touched germs, now I’m afraid I’ll get sick.” It’s more… I’ll touch something, or think I may have touched something unclean, and then this thought starts pressing at me that I could carry it somewhere else or pass it along without realizing it.

For example, I might be reading at home, and suddenly I’ll get this ugly little thought that I’ve left something unsafe or contaminated somehow. Or when I’m getting ready for a museum shift, I’ll start wondering whether I touched something unclean before leaving, and then I picture myself bringing that risk with me. Not in a very logical, step-by-step way, really. It just barges in and feels urgent.

And I do know, sitting here talking about it, that it’s out of proportion. I know perfectly well that most people would just move on and not give it a second thought. But in the moment it’s hard to let go of, because it feels like if I ignore it, I might be putting someone at risk.
Do you often worry that you might contaminate someone else with germs or illness through your actions?

Yes, that’s exactly the sort of thing I mean. It isn’t usually that I think, “I’m going to become ill,” so much as, “What if I’ve touched something unclean and then carried it to someone else?” That’s the thought that gets its hooks in.

It can happen at very ordinary times. I’ll be sitting at home reading, not doing anything risky, and suddenly this ugly little thought barges in that I may have left something unsafe, or that something has been contaminated somehow. Or I’ll be getting ready to go in for a museum shift, and I’ll start wondering whether I touched something unclean before leaving, and then whether I might bring that with me and expose someone else.

I know perfectly well, when I step back from it, that it’s out of proportion. I’m not saying there’s a clear chain of evidence in my mind. It’s more like this sharp doubt, this feeling that I could have put someone at risk through something small I did or didn’t do. And then it feels hard to just ignore it, because ignoring it feels almost like being irresponsible.
Have your symptoms been causing you significant distress or problems in your daily life, such as interfering with your relationships, work, or other activities?

Yes, I would say it has, though I’m still managing, mostly. I live on my own and I do get through the day, and I don’t want to make it sound as if everything has collapsed, because it hasn’t. But it does interfere.

The main thing is getting out the door. These little routines and checks can stretch on much longer than I mean them to. I’ll think, “Right, I’m leaving now,” and then something catches in my mind and I feel I have to go back over it. And then suddenly I’m not leaving now, I’m leaving ten or fifteen minutes later, or more, and I’m flustered before I’ve even arrived.

It has made me late to some of my docent shifts at the museum, which I hate, because I try to be reliable. And there have been a few museum events I just didn’t go to, not because I didn’t want to go, but because by the time I was trying to get ready and out of the house, it all felt like too much. So yes, it’s not disabling in the sense that I can’t function, but it definitely causes distress and it does get in the way of things I care about.
Have your symptoms caused you any problems with your daily life or relationships that you feel are significant?

Yes, I think so. I mean, I’m still managing on my own day to day — I don’t want to overstate it as if I can’t function — but it does get in the way in ways that matter to me.

The clearest example is getting out of the house. I’ll be trying to leave for one of my docent shifts, and then the routines or checking or just needing to feel sure about things will start taking longer than I expected. It’s not dramatic from the outside, probably, but suddenly I’m ten or fifteen minutes behind, and then I arrive late and already upset with myself.

And there have been a few museum events I skipped altogether, not because I didn’t want to go. I did want to go. But getting ready and actually getting out the door felt like too much by that point, and I just… didn’t make it. That bothers me, because the museum is important to me, and I like being dependable. So yes, even though I’m still living independently and handling things, it has caused problems that feel significant to me.

It isn’t that I truly believe, in a clear-headed way, that if I don’t check the stove one more time the house will definitely burn down, or if I don’t wash my hands again after adjusting my wrist brace something terrible will happen. But in the moment, there’s this pressure—almost like I can’t quite move on until I’ve completed the little routine. I’ll wash my hands, then touch or handle the brace, and then I feel pulled to wash them again, even if I know there’s no real reason. And the counting is similar. Before I leave, I sometimes silently count through steps in my head, like I’m making sure everything has been accounted for. It gives me a bit of relief, I suppose, or at least it quiets that anxious feeling for the moment. But then it also makes me late, which is maddening, because I can see what’s happening and still feel like I have to finish it before I can walk out the door.
